It is to be observed, however, that although no one individual christian Minister can, with complete certainty, trace his own succession in an unbroken chain from the Apostles, and prove that there was no flaw in any link, the case is different when we look to the Clergy generally. For there can be no reasonable doubt that such an Order of men did always exist, from the times of the Apostles, continuously, to this day. We may be as sure of this as we are that great numbers of the English nation are descendants of the Saxons, who settled in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in the fifth and sixth centuries, though there is probably no one man who could trace his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from any of them. For, christian Ministers held office in the churches as immediate successors of others who held the same office, and who in like manner professed to be the immediate successors of others, &c., whose predecessors had been appointed by the Apostles themselves. Now if, a century ago, or ten centuries ago, or at any other time, a number of men had arisen, claiming to be the immediate successors (as above described) of persons holding this office, when, in fact, no such Order of men had ever been heard of, such an absurd pretension would have been immediately exposed and derided. There must always, therefore, have existed such an Order of men, from the time of those Apostles who professed to be eye-witnesses of the Resurrection, and to work sensible public miracles in proof of their divine commission. And, consequently, the christian Ministry is a standing monument to attest the public <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> of those miraculous events at the very time when they are said to have occurred. Now, at that time there must have been great numbers of persons able and willing to expose the imposture, had there been any. And this argument for the truth of the Sacred History is quite independent of any particular mode of appointing christian Ministers. If, for instance, these had always been elected by the People, and had at once entered on their office without any ordination by other Ministers, still, if they were but appointed (in whatever mode) as immediate successors of persons holding the same office, the argument would be the same. That mode, indeed, of admitting men into the Ministry which was practised by the Apostles (1 Tim. iv. 14, and v. 22) has, in fact, been retained in all ages of Christianity. But the argument we have now been considering is quite independent of this. It turns entirely on the mere fact of the constant existence of a certain Order of men. And it is worth observing, that the Lord's Day is a monument of the same kind. It is kept all over the world, by different and even hostile Bodies of Christians, in memory of the Resurrection of Jesus Christ. And not only so,—for this alone would not be a decisive proof,—but it is observed by them as a day which has been always thus kept, from the very day when the Lord Jesus is recorded to have risen, and to have appeared to his Disciples. Now, if it had not been thus constantly kept, from the first, but the observance of it introduced in some later age, those among whom it was thus introduced would have been able to testify that they had never heard of such a festival before.

HOBBS

Pages 340-344

Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury may be numbered among those eminent persons born in the latter half of the sixteenth century, who gave a new character to European <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in the succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was one of the late writers and late learners. It was not till he was 1 The same commonplace paradoxes were retailed by the Sophists, whom <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> is introduced as chastising in the Dialogues of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>. They were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enough to be put by the historian into the mouth of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> in a public speech. 2 "Et hæc quidem locum aliquem haberent, eliam si daretur (quo sine summo scele re dari nequit) non esse Deum, aut non curari <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> eo negotia humana." (Proleg. II.) And in another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, "Jus naturale est dictatum rectae rationis, indicans actui aliqui, ex ejus convenientia aut disconvenientia cum ipsa natura rationali et sociali, inesse moralem turpitudinem aut necessitatem moralem, ac consequenter ab auctore naturæ Deo talcm actum aut vetari aut praepiri. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTUS">Actus</a> de quibus tale existat dictatum, debiti sunt aut illiciti per se, atque idea Deo necessario praecipi aut vetiti intelliguntur." (Lib. I. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. i. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 16.) 3 Born in 1588; died in 1679. 4 <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, Descartes, Hobbes, and Grotius. The writings of the first are still as delightful and wonderful as they ever were, and his authority <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> have no end. Descartes forms an era in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, of Physics, of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>. The controversies excited by Grotius have <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> ceased, but the powerful influence of his works will be doubted by those only who are unacquainted with the disputes of the seventeenth century. nearly thirty that he supplied the defects of his early <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, by classical studies so successfully prosecuted, that he wrote well in the Latin then used by his scientific contemporaries; and made such proficiency in Greek as, in his earliest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the Translation of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>, published when he was forty, to afford a specimen of a version still valued for its remarkable fidelity; though written with a stiffness and constraint very opposite to the masterly facility of his original compositions. It was after forty that he learned the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> (so miserably defective was his education); but yielding to the paradoxical disposition apt to infect those who begin to learn after the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> age of commencement, he exposed himself, by absurd controversies with the masters of a science which looks <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with scorn on the Sophist. A considerable portion of his mature age was passed on the Continent, where he travelled as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to two successive Earls of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>; a family with whom he seems to have passed near half a century of his long <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In France his reputation, founded at that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> solely on personal intercourse, became so <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that his observations on the Meditations of Descartes were published in the works of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, together with those of Gassendi and Arnauld. It was about his sixtieth year that he began to publish those philosophical writings which contain his peculiar opinions—which set the understanding of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> into general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and stirred up controversies among metaphysicians and moralists, not even yet determined. At the age of eighty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> he had the boldness to publish metrical versions of the Iliad and Odyssey, which the greatness of his name, and the singularity of the undertaking, still render objects of curiosity, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not of criticism. He owed his influence to various causes; at the head of which may be placed that genius for system, which, though it cramps the growth of knowledge, perhaps finally atones for that mischief, by the zeal and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> which it rouses among followers and opponents, who discover <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> by accident, when in pursuit of weapons for their warfare. A system which attempts a task so hard as that of subjecting vast provinces of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> knowledge to one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> two principles, if it presents some striking instances of conformity to superficial appearances, is sure to delight the framer; and, for a time, to subdue and captivate the student too entirely for sober reflection and rigorous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>. The evil does not indeed very frequently recur. Perhaps <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, Hobbes, and Kant, are the only persons who united in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the great faculties of comprehension and discrimination which compose the Genius of System. Of the three, Aristotle alone could throw it off where it was glaringly unsuitable; and it is deserving of observation, that the reign of system seems, from these examples, progressively to shorten in proportion as reason is cultivated and knowledge advances. But, in the first instance, consistency passes for truth. When principles in some instances have proved sufficient to give an unexpected explanation of facts, the delighted reader is content to accept as true all other deductions from the principles. Specious premises being assumed to be true, nothing more can be required than logical inference. Mathematical forms <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> current as the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> of mathematical certainty. The unwary admirer is satisfied with the completeness and symmetry of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>—unmindful of the need of examining the firmness of the foundation and the soundness of the materials. The system-maker, like the conqueror, long dazzles and overawes the world; but when their sway is past, the vulgar herd, unable to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> their astonishing faculties, take <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> by trampling on fallen greatness. The dogmatism of Hobbes was, however unjustly, one of the sources of his fame. The founders of systems deliver their novelties with the undoubting spirit of discoverers; and their --- 1 The prevalence of freethinking under <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII., to a far greater degree than it was avowed, appears not only from the complaints of Mersenne and of Grotius, but from the disclosures of Guy Patin; who, in his Letters, describes his own conversations with Gassendi and Naudé, so as to leave no doubt of their opinions. 2 "Another <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>," says the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a>, "is the over-early and peremptory <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of knowledge into arts and methods, from which time <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> receives small augmentation." (Bacon's Advancement of Learning, book i.) "Method," says he, "carrying a show of total and perfect knowledge, has a tendency to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> acquiescence." What pregnant words! followers are apt to be dogmatical, because they can see nothing beyond their own ground. It might seem incredible, if it were not established by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of all ages, that those who differ most from the opinions of their fellow-men are most confident of the truth of their own. But it commonly requires an overweening conceit of the superiority of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s own judgment, to make him espouse very singular notions; and when he has once embraced them, they are endeared to him by the hostility of those whom he contemns as the prejudiced vulgar. The temper of Hobbes must have been originally haughty. The advanced age at which he published his obnoxious opinions, rendered him more impatient of the acrimonious opposition which they necessarily provoked; until at length a strong <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the injustice of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> impending over his head, for the publication of what he believed to be truth, cooperated with the peevishness and timidity of his years, to render him the most imperious and morose of dogmatists. His dogmatism has indeed one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> more offensive than that of most others. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">Propositions</a> the most adverse to the opinions of mankind, and the most abhorrent from their feelings, are introduced into the course of his argument with mathematical coldness. He presents them as demonstrated conclusions, without deigning to explain to his fellow-creatures how they all happened to believe the opposite absurdities; without even the compliment of once observing how widely his discoveries were at variance with the most <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and universal judgments of the human understanding. The same quality in Spinoza indicates a recluse's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the world. In Hobbes it is the arrogance of a man who knows mankind and despises them. A permanent foundation of his fame consists in his admirable style, which seems to be the very perfection of didactic <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Short, clear, precise, pithy, his language never has more than one meaning, which never requires a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> thought to find. By the help of his exact method, it takes so firm a hold on the mind, that it will not allow <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLACKEN">slacken</a>. His little tract on Human <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> has scarcely an ambiguous or a needless word. He has so great a power of always choosing the most significant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a>, that he never is reduced to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> expedient of using many in its stead. He had so thoroughly studied the genius of the language, and knew so well to steer between pedantry and vulgarity, that two centuries have not superannuated probably more than a dozen of his words. His expressions are so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a>, that he is clear without the help of illustration. Perhaps no writer of any age or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, on subjects so abstruse, has manifested an equal power of engraving his thoughts on the mind of his readers. He seems never to have taken a word for ornament or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; and he deals with eloquence and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> as the natural philosopher who explains the mechanism of children's toys, or deigns to contrive them. Yet his style so stimulates attention, that it never tires; and, to those who are acquainted with the subject, appears to have as much spirit as can be safely blended with reason. He compresses his thoughts so unaffectedly, and yet so tersely, as to produce occasionally maxims which excite the same agreeable surprise with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and have become a sort of philosophical proverbs; the success of which he partly owed to the suitableness of such forms of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> to his dictatorial nature. His words have such an appearance of springing from his thoughts, as to impress on the reader a strong <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his originality, and indeed to prove that he was not conscious of borrowing; though conversation with Gassendi must have influenced his mind; and it is hard to believe that his coincidence with Ockham should have been purely accidental, on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> so important as the denial of general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, the reference of moral distinctions to superior power, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> thraldom of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> under the civil power, which he seems to have thought necessary, to maintain that independence of the state on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> with which Ockham had been contented. His philosophical writings might be read without reminding any one that the author was more than an intellectual machine. They never betray a feeling except that insupportable arrogance which looks down on men as a lower <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of beings; whose almost unanimous hostility is so far from shaking the firmness of his conviction, or even ruffling the calmness of his contempt, that it appears too petty a circumstance to require explanation, or even to merit notice. Let it not be forgotten, that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his renown depends on the application of his admirable powers to expound truth when he meets it. This great merit is conspicuous in that part of his treatise of Human Nature which relates to the percipient and reasoning faculties. It is also very remarkable in many of his secondary principles on the subject of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which, while the first principles are false and dangerous, are as admirable for truth as for his accustomed and unrivalled propriety of expression. In many of these observations he even shows a disposition to soften his paradoxes, and to conform to the common sense of mankind. It was with perfect truth observed by my excellent friend Mr Stewart, that "the ethical principles of Hobbes are completely interwoven with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> system." He might have said, that the whole of Hobbes's system, moral, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, and in part philosophical, depended on his political scheme; not indeed logically, as conclusions depend on premises, but (if the word may be excused) psychologically, as the formation of one opinion may be influenced by a disposition to adapt it to previously cherished opinions. The Translation of Thucydides, as he himself boasts, was published to show the evils of popular government. Men he represented as being originally equal, and having an equal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to all things, but as being taught by reason to sacrifice this right for the advantages of peace, and to submit to a common authority, which can preserve quiet, only by being the sole depository of force, and must therefore be absolute and unlimited. The supreme authority cannot be sufficient for its purpose, unless it be wielded by a single <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; nor even then, unless his absolute power extends over religion, which may prompt men to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> by the fear of an evil greater than <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The perfect state of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, according to him, is where law prescribes the religion and morality of the people, and where the will of an absolute sovereign is the sole fountain of law. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOOKER">Hooker</a> had inculcated the simple truth, that "to live by one man's will is the cause of many men's misery." Hobbes embraced the daring <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a>, that to live by one man's will is the only means of all men's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. Having thus rendered religion the slave of every human <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, it was an unavoidable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, that he should be disposed to lower her character, and lessen her power over men; that he should regard atheism as the most effectual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of preventing rebellion; at least that species of rebellion which prevailed in his time, and had excited his alarms. The formidable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> of religion with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> haunted his mind, and urged him to the bold attempt of rooting out both these mighty principles; which, when combined with interests and passions, when debased by impure support, and provoked by unjust resistance, have indeed the power of fearfully agitating <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; but which are, nevertheless, in their own nature, and as far as they are unmixed and undisturbed, the fountains of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, of order, of peace, as well as of those moral hopes, and of those glorious aspirations after higher excellence, which encourage and exalt the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> in its passage through misery and depravity. A Hobbist is the only consistent persecutor; for he alone considers himself as bound, by whatever <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> he has remaining, to conform to the religion of the sovereign. --- 1 See De Corpore Politico, Part i. chap. ii. iii. iv. and Leviathan, Part i. chap. xiv. xv. for remarks of this sort, full of sagacity. 2 "The laws of nature are immutable and eternal; for injustice, ingratitude, arrogance, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, iniquity, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACCEPTION">acception</a> of persons, and the rest, can never be made lawful. For it can never be that <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> shall preserve life, and peace destroy it." (Leviathan, Part i. chap. xv. See also Part ii. chap. xxvi. xxviii. on Laws, and on Punishments.) 3 See Dissertation First, p. 42. The political state of England is indeed said by himself to have occasioned his first philosophical publication. Nascitur interea aeolus excercare bellum. Horreo spectans, Meque <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> dilectam confero Lutetiam, Posteque duos annos edo De Cive Libellum. (Pits Hobbesis.) 4 The speech of Euphemus in the 6th book of that historian, and the conference between the ministers from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and the Melean chiefs, in the 5th book, exhibit an undisguised Hobbes, which was very dramatically put into the mouth of Athenian statesmen at a time when, as we learn from Plato and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, it was preached by the Sophists. He claims from others no more than he is himself ready to yield to any master; while the religionist who persecutes a member of another <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, exacts the sacrifice of conscience and sincerity, though professing that, rather than make it himself, he is prepared to die.

HUTCHESON

Pages 371-382

This ingenious writer began to try his own strength by private Letters, written in his early youth to Dr Clarke, the metaphysical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>; on whom young philosophers seem to have considered themselves as possessing a claim, which he had too much goodness to reject. His correspondence with Hutcheson is lost; but we may judge of its spirit by his answers to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-BUTLER">Butler</a>, and by one to Mr Henry Home, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames, then a young adventurer in the prevalent speculations. Nearly at the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> with Butler's first publication, the writings of Hutcheson began to show coincidences with him, indicative of the tendency of moral <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> to a new form, to which an impulse had been given by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SHAFTESBURY">Shaftesbury</a>, and which was roused to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> by the adverse system of Clarke. Lord Molesworth, the friend of Shaftesbury, patronised Hutcheson, and even criticised his manuscript. Though a Presbyterian, he was befriended by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a>, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, himself a metaphysician; and he was aided by Mr Synge, afterwards a bishop, to whom speculations somewhat similar to his own had occurred. Butler and Hutcheson coincided in the two important positions, that disinterested affections, and a distinct moral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, are essential parts of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Hutcheson is a chaste and simple writer, who imbibed the opinions, without the literary faults of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, Shaftesbury. He has a clearness of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and fulness of illustration, which are wanting in Butler. But he is inferior to both these writers in the appearance at least of originality, and to Butler especially in that philosophical courage which, when it discovers the fountains of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and falsehood, leaves others to follow the streams. He states as strongly as Butler, that "the same cause which determines us to pursue <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> for ourselves, determines us both to esteem and benevolence on their proper occasions—even the very frame of our nature." It is vain, as he justly observes, for the patrons of a refined selfishness to pretend that we pursue the happiness of others for the sake of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> which we derive from it; since it is apparent that there could be no such pleasure <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there had been no previous affection. "Had we no affection distinct from self-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, nothing could raise a desire of the happiness of others, but when viewed as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> of our own." He seems to have been the first who entertained <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> notions of the formation of the secondary desires, which had been overlooked by Butler. "There must arise, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of our original desires, secondary desires of every thing useful to gratify the primary desire. Thus, as soon as we apprehend the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of wealth <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> power to gratify our original desires, we also desire them. From their universality as means arises the general prevalence of these desires of wealth and power." Proceeding farther in his zeal against the selfish system than Lord Shaftesbury, who seems ultimately to rest the reasonableness of benevolence on its subserviency to the happiness of the individual, he represents the moral faculty to be, as well as self-love and benevolence, a calm general impulse, which may and does impel a good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> to sacrifice not only happiness, but even <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> itself, to virtue. As Mr Locke had spoken of an internal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>,—Lord Shaftesbury once or twice of a reflex <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and once of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral sense</a>,—Hutcheson, who had a steadier, if not a clearer view of the nature of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> than Butler, calls it a Moral Sense; a name which quickly became popular, and continues to be a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. By sense, he understood a capacity of receiving <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, together with pleasures and pains, from a class of --- 1 Born in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> in 1694; died at Glasgow in 1747. 2 Woodhouselee's Life of Lord Kames, vol. I. Append. No. 3. 3 The first edition of Butler's Sermons was published in 1726, in which year also appeared the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of Hutcheson's Inquiry into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">Beauty</a> and Virtue. The Sermons had been preached some years before, though there is no likelihood that the contents could have reached a young teacher at Dublin. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Hutcheson's birth is not mentioned in any account known to me. Ireland may be truly said to be "inscrutabili." 4 Inquiry, p. 152. 5 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the Passions, p. 17. 6 Ibid. p. 8. objects. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> moral was used to describe the particular class in question. It implied only that conscience was a separate element in our nature, and that it was not a state or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the understanding. According to him, it also implied that it was an original and implanted principle; but every other part of his theory might be embraced by those who hold it to be derivative. The object of moral approbation, according to him, is general benevolence; and he carries this generous <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> so far as to deny that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> as it regards ourselves, can be morally approved;—an assertion contradicted by every man's feelings, and to which we owe the Dissertation on the Nature of Virtue which Butler annexed to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">Analogy</a>. By proving that all virtuous actions produce general good, he fancied that he had proved the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of regarding the general good in every act of virtue;—an instance of that confusion of the theory of moral sentiments with the criterion of moral actions, against which the reader was warned at the opening of this Dissertation, as fatal to Ethical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>. He is chargeable, like Butler, with a vicious circle, in describing virtuous acts as those which are approved by the moral sense, while he at the same time describes the moral sense as the faculty which perceives and feels the morality of actions. He was the father of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> philosophy in Scotland, at least in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times; for though in the beginning of the sixteenth century the Scotch are said to have been known throughout <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> by their unmeasured <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for dialectical subtleties,¹ and though this metaphysical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> was nourished by the controversies which followed the Reformation, yet it languished, with every other intellectual taste and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, from the Restoration, first silenced by civil disorders, and afterwards repressed by an exemplary but unlettered clergy, till the philosophy of Shaftesbury was brought by Hutcheson from Ireland. We are told by the writer of his Life, (a fine piece of philosophical biography) that "he had a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of rational enthusiasm for learning, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, virtue, and human happiness;"² that he taught in public with persuasive eloquence; that his instructive conversation was at once lively and modest; that he united pure manners with a kind disposition. What wonder that such a man should have spread the love of knowledge and virtue around him, and should have rekindled in his adopted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> a relish for the sciences which he cultivated! To him may also be ascribed that proneness to multiply ultimate and original principles in human nature, which characterized the Scottish School till the second extinction of a passion for metaphysical speculation in Scotland. A careful perusal of the writings of this now little studied <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> satisfy the well-qualified reader, that Dr <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Smith's ethical speculations are not so unsuggested as they are beautiful. BERKELEY.³ This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> metaphysician was so little a moralist, that it requires the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of his name to excuse its introduction here. His Theory of Vision contains a great discovery in mental philosophy. His immaterialism is chiefly valuable as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOUCHSTONE">touchstone</a> of metaphysical sagacity; showing those to be altogether without it, who, like Johnson and Beattie, believed that his speculations were sceptical, that they implied any distrust in the senses, or that they had the smallest ¹ The character given of the Scotch by the famous and unfortunate Servetus, in his edition of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, (1533) is in many respects curious. "Gallis amicissimi, Anglorumque regi maxime infestis. Subita ingenia, et in ultimum proma, ferociaque. In bello fortis, inedia, vigiliae, angoria patientissimae. In scienti forma sed cultui negligentiori; invidi natura et ceterorum mortalium contemptores; ostentant plus simile sollicitatem summae, et in summa etiam egestate summa gracia <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> regem stipem referunt, nec non dialecticis argutissimis sibi blandiuntur."—Subita ingenia is an expression <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the "Prefervidum Scotorum ingenium" of Buchanan. Churchill almost agrees in words with Servetus: Whose lineage <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> From great and glorious, though forgotten kings. And the strong antipathy of the late King George III. to what he called "Scotch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>," proves the permanency of the last part of the national character. ² Life by Dr Lexchman, prefixed to Hutcheson's System of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral Philosophy</a>, 1755. ³ Born near <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THOMASTOWN">Thomastown</a> in Ireland, in 1684; died at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1753. tendency to disturb reasoning or alter conduct. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> learning, exact science, polished <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, modern literature, and the fine arts, contributed to adorn and enrich the mind of this accomplished man. All his contemporaries agreed with the satirist in ascribing To Berkeley every virtue under heaven. Adverse factions and hostile wits concurred only in loving, admiring, and contributing to advance him. The severe sense of Swift endured his visions; the modest Addison endeavored to reconcile Clarke to his ambitious speculations. His character converted the satire of Pope into fervid praise. Even the discerning, fastidious, and turbulent Atterbury said, after an interview with him, "So much understanding, so much knowledge, so much innocence, and such humility, I did not think had been the portion of any but <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, till I <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>." Lord <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHURST">Bathurst</a> told me, that the Members of the Scriblerus Club being met at his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at dinner, they agreed to rally Berkeley, who was also his guest, on his scheme at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERMUDAS">Bermudas</a>. Berkeley, having listened to the many lively things they had to say, begged to be heard in his turn, and displayed his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> with such an astonishing and animating force of eloquence and enthusiasm, that they were struck dumb, and after some pause, rose all up together, with earnestness exclaiming, "Let us set out with him immediately." It was when thus beloved and celebrated that he conceived, at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of forty-five, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of devoting his life to reclaim and convert the natives of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; and he employed as much influence and solicitation as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> men do for their most prized objects, in obtaining leave to resign his dignities and revenues, to quit his accomplished and affectionate friends, and to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-BURY">bury</a> himself in what must have seemed an intellectual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. After four years' residence at Newport in Rhode <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, he was compelled, by the refusal of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a> to furnish him with funds for his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, to forego his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of heroic, or rather godlike benevolence; though not without some consoling forethought of the fortune of the country where he had sojourned. Westward the course of empire takes its way, The first four acts already past, A fifth shall <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the drama with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, Time's noblest offspring is its last. Thus disappointed in his ambition of keeping a School for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> children, at a salary of a hundred pounds by the year, he was received, on his return, with open arms by the philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, at whose metaphysical parties he made one with Sherlock, who, as well as Smalridge, was his supporter, and with Hoadley, who, following Clarke, was his antagonist. By her influence, he was made bishop of Cloyne. It is one of his highest boasts, that though of English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, he was a true Irishman, and the first eminent Protestant, after the unhappy contest at the Revolution, who avowed his love for all his countrymen. He asked, "Whether their habitations and furniture were not more sordid than those of the savage Americans?" "Whether a scheme for the welfare of this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a> should not take in the whole inhabitants?" and, "Whether it was a vain attempt, to project the flourishing of our Protestant gentry, exclusive of the bulk of the natives?" He proceeds to promote the reformation suggested in this pregnant question by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of Queries, intimating, with the utmost skill and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, every reason that proves the necessity, and the safety, and the wisest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of adopting his suggestion. He contributed, by a truly Christian address to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, to their perfect quiet during the rebellion of 1745; and soon after published a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the clergy of that persuasion, beseeching them to inculcate industry among their flocks, for which he received their thanks. He tells them, that it was a saying among the negro slaves, "if negro were not negro, Irishman would be negro." It is difficult to read these proofs of benevolence and foresight without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, at the moment when, after a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> of near a century, his suggestions have been at length, at the close of a struggle of twenty-five years, adopted, by the admis- --- 1 Duncombe's Letters, 106, 107. 2 Warton on Pope. 3 See his Querist, 353; published in 1735. 4 Ibid. 255. 5 April 1829. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">sion</a> of the whole Irish nation to the privileges of the British <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">Constitution</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a> of Berkeley was not, like that of Swift, tainted by disappointed ambition; nor was it, like Swift's, confined to a colony of English <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. Perhaps the Querist contains more hints, then original, still unapplied in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">legislation</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> economy, than are to be found in any equal space. From the writings of his advanced years, when he chose a medical Tract\(^1\) to be the vehicle of his philosophical reflections, though it cannot be said that he relinquished his early opinions, it is at least apparent that his mind had received a new bent, and was habitually turned from reasoning towards <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>. His immaterialism indeed modestly appears, but only to purify and elevate our thoughts, and to fix them on Mind, the paramount and primeval principle of all things. "Perhaps," says he, "the truth about innate ideas may be, that there are properly no ideas or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> objects in the mind but what are derived from sense, but that there are also, besides these, her own acts and operations—such are notions;" a statement which seems once more to admit general conceptions, and which might have served, as well as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> passage of Leibnitz, as the basis of the modern philosophy of Germany. From these compositions of his old age, he appears then to have recurred with fondness to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and the later Platonists; writers from whose <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> reasonings an intellect so acute could hardly hope for an argumentative satisfaction of all its difficulties, and whom he probably rather studied as a means of inuring his mind to objects beyond the visible diurnal sphere, and of attaching it, through frequent meditation, to that perfect and transcendent goodness to which his moral feelings always pointed, and which they incessantly strove to grasp. His mind, enlarging as it rose, at length receives every theist, however imperfect his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> in its philosophic piety. "Truth," he beautifully concludes, "is the cry of all, but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> of a few. Certainly, where it is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> passion, it does not give way to vulgar cares, nor is it contented with a little ardour in the early time of life; <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> perhaps to pursue, but not so fit to weigh and revise. He that would make a real progress in knowledge, must dedicate his age as well as youth, the later growth as well as first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, at the altar of Truth." So did Berkeley, and such were almost his latest words. His general principles of Ethics may be shortly stated in his own words:—"As God is a being of infinite goodness, his end is the good of his creatures. The general wellbeing of all men of all nations, of all ages of the world, is that which he designs should be procured by the concurrence actions of each individual." Having stated that this end can be pursued only in one of two ways—either by computing the consequences of each <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, or by obeying rules which generally tend to happiness—and having shown the first to be impossible, he rightly infers, "that the end to which God requires the concurrence of human actions, must be carried on by the observation of certain determinate and universal rules or moral precepts, which in their own nature have a necessary tendency to promote the wellbeing of mankind, taking in all nations and ages, from the beginning to the end of the world."* A <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>, of which a journey to an Utopia, in the centre of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, forms the chief part, called The Adventures of Signor Gaudentio di <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, has been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> ascribed to him; probably on no other ground than its union of pleasing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> with benevolence and elegance.\(^2\) Of the exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> and beauty of his diction, no man accustomed to English <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> can need to be informed. His works are, beyond dispute, the finest models of philosophical style since Cicero. Perhaps they surpass those of the orator, in the wonderful art by which the fullest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> is thrown on the most minute and evanescent parts of the most subtile of human conceptions. Perhaps he also surpassed Cicero in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> of simplicity, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> eminently found in Irish writers before the end of the eighteenth century; conspicuous in the masculine severity of Swift, --- \(^1\) Siris, or Reflections on Tar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">Water</a>. \(^2\) Sermon in Trinity College Chapel, on Passive Obedience, 1712. \(^3\) Gentleman's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1777. in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> fancy of Berkeley, in the native tenderness and elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOLDSMITH">Goldsmith</a>, and not withholding its attractions from Hutcheson and Leland, writers of classical taste, though of inferior power. The two Irish philosophers of the eighteenth century may be said to have co-operated in calling forth the metaphysical genius of Scotland; for, though Hutcheson spread the taste, and furnished the principles, yet Berkeley undoubtedly produced the scepticism of Hume, which stimulated the instinctive school to activity, and was thought incapable of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONFUTATION">confutation</a>, otherwise than by their doctrines. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">DAVID</a> HUME The Life of Mr Hume, written by himself, is remarkable above most, if not all writings of that sort, for hitting the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> between coldness and egotism which becomes a modest man in speaking of his private <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Few writers, whose opinions were so obnoxious, have more perfectly escaped every personal imputation. Very few men of so calm a character have been so warmly beloved. That he approached to the character of a perfectly good and wise man, is an affectionate exaggeration, for which his friend Dr Smith, in the first moments of his sorrow, may well be excused. But such a praise can never be earned without passing through either of the extremes of fortune; without standing the test of temptations, dangers, and sacrifices. It may be said with truth, that the private character of Mr Hume exhibited all the virtues which a man of reputable station, under a mild government, in the quiet times of a civilized country, has often the opportunity to practise. He showed no want of the qualities which fit men for more severe trials. Though others had warmer affections, no man was a kinder relation, a more unwearied friend, or more free from meanness and malice. His character was so simple, that he did not even affect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>; but neither his friendships nor his deportment were changed by a fame which filled all Europe. His good nature, his plain manners, and his active kindness, procured him at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> the enviable name of the good David, from a society not so alive to goodness, as without reason to place it at the head of the qualities of a celebrated man. His whole character is faithfully and touchingly represented in the story of La Roche, where Mr Mackenzie, without concealing Mr Hume's opinions, brings him into contact with scenes of tender piety, and yet preserves the interest inspired by genuine and unalloyed, though moderated feelings and affections. The amiable and venerable patriarch of Scottish Literature was averse from the opinions of the philosopher on whom he has composed this best <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. He tells us that he read the manuscript to Dr Smith, "who declared he did not find a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> to object to, but added, with his characteristic absence of mind, that he was surprised he had never heard of the anecdote before." So lively was the delineation thus sanctioned by the most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> of all testimonies. Mr Mackenzie indulges his own <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> feelings by modestly intimating, that Dr Smith's answer seemed to justify the last words of the tale, "that there were moments when the philosopher recalled to his mind the venerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the good La Roche, and wished that he had never doubted." To those who are strangers to the seductions of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a>, to the intoxication of fame, and to the bewitchment of prohibited opinions, it must be unaccountable, that he who revered benevolence should, without apparent regret, cease to see it on the Throne of the Universe. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of wonder that his habitual esteem for every fragment and shadow of moral excellence should not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him to envy those who contemplated its perfection in that living and paternal character which gives it a power over the human heart. On the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, if we had no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> --- 1 Born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in 1711; died there in 1776. 2 Dr Smith's Letter to Mr Strahan, annexed to the Life of Hume. 3 See Notes and Illustrations, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTE">note</a> P. 4 Mirror, Nos. 42, 43, 44. 5 Mackenzie's Life of John Home, p. 21. of the power of opposite opinions in producing irreconcilable animosities, we might have hoped that those who retained such <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> privileges would have looked with more compassion than dislike on a virtuous man who had lost them. In such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it is too little remembered, that repugnance to hypocrisy, and impatience of long concealment, are the qualities of the best formed minds; and that, if the publication of some doctrines proves often painful and mischievous, the habitual suppression of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is injurious to reason, and very dangerous to sincerity. Practical questions thus arise, so difficult and perplexing, that their determination generally depends on the boldness or timidity of the individual,—on his tenderness for the feelings of the good, or his greater reverence for the free <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of reason. The time is not yet come when the noble maxim of Plato, "that every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is unwillingly deprived of truth," will be practically and heartily applied by men to the honest opponents who differ from them most widely. In his twenty-seventh year he published at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> the Treatise of Human Nature, the first systematic attack on all the principles of knowledge and belief, and the most formidable, if universal scepticism could ever be more than a mere exercise of ingenuity. This memorable work was reviewed in a Journal of that time, in a criticism not distinguished by ability, which affects to represent the style of a very clear writer as unintelligible—sometimes from a purpose to insult, but oftener from sheer dulness—which is unaccountably silent respecting the consequences of a sceptical system; and which concludes with a prophecy so much at variance with the general tone of the article, that it would seem to be added by a different hand. "It bears incontestable marks of a great capacity, of a soaring genius, but young, and not yet thoroughly practised. Time and use may <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> these qualities in the author, and we shall probably have reason to consider this, compared with his later productions, in the same light as we view the juvenile works of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, or the first manner of Raphael." The great speculator did not, in this work, amuse himself, like Bayle, with dialectical exercises, which only inspire a disposition towards doubt, by showing in detail the uncertainty of most opinions. He aimed at proving, not that nothing was known, but that nothing could be known;—from the structure of the understanding to demonstrate, that we are doomed for ever to dwell in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and universal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. It is true that such a system of universal scepticism never can be more than an intellectual amusement, an exercise of subtilty; of which the only use is to check dogmatism, but which perhaps oftener provokes and produces that much more common evil. As those dictates of experience which regulate conduct must be the objects of belief, all objections which attack them in common with the principles of reasoning must be utterly ineffectual. Whatever attacks every principle of belief can destroy none. As long as the foundations of knowledge are allowed to remain on the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> (be it called of certainty or uncertainty) with the maxims of life, the whole system of human conviction must continue undisturbed. When the sceptic boasts of having involved the results of experience and the elements of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> in the same ruin with the doctrines of religion and the principles of philosophy, he may be answered, That no dogmatist ever claimed more than the same degree of certainty for these various convictions and opinions; and that his scepticism, therefore, leaves them in the relative condition in which it found them. No man knew better, or owned more frankly than Mr Hume, that to --- 1 Sextus, a physician of the empirical, i.e. anti-theoretical school, who lived at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in the reign of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>, has preserved the reasonings of the ancient Sceptics as they were to be found in their most improved state, in the writings of Encideimus, a Cretan, who was a Professor in the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, soon after the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> into a Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. The greater part of the grounds of doubt are very shallow and popular. There are, among them, intimations of the argument against a necessary connection of causes with effects, afterwards better presented by Glanville in his Sceptics Scientifica. See Notes and Illustrations, note Q. 2 History of the Works of the Learned, November and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1739, p. 353-404. This Review is attributed by some (Chalmers, Biographical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>) to Warburton, but certainly without foundation. this answer there is no serious reply. Universal scepticism involves a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> in terms. It is a belief that there can be no belief. It is an attempt of the mind to act without its structure, and by other laws than those to which its nature has subjected its operations. To reason without assenting to the principles on which reasoning is founded, is not unlike an effort to feel without nerves, or to move without muscles. No man can be allowed to be an opponent in reasoning, who does not set out with admitting all the principles, without the admission of which it is impossible to reason.1 It is indeed a puerile, nay, in the eye of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, a childish play, to attempt either to establish or to confute principles by argument, which every step of that argument must presuppose. The only <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the two cases is, that he who tries to prove them can do so only by first taking them for granted; and that he who attempts to impugn them falls at the very first step into a contradiction, from which he never can rise. It must, however, be allowed, that universal scepticism has practical consequences of a very mischievous nature. This is because its universality is not steadily kept in view, and constantly borne in mind. If it were, the above short and plain remark would be an effectual antidote to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POISON">poison</a>. But in practice, it is an armoury from which weapons are taken to be employed against some opinions, while it is hidden from notice that the same weapon would equally cut <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> every other conviction. It is thus that Mr Hume's theory of causation is used as an answer to arguments for the existence of the Deity, without warning the reader that it would equally lead him not to expect that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> will rise to-morrow. It must also be added, that those who are early accustomed to dispute first principles are never likely to acquire, in a sufficient degree, that earnestness and that sincerity, that strong love of truth, and that conscientious solicitude for the formation of just opinions, which are not the least virtues of men, but of which the cultivation is the more especial duty of all who call themselves philosophers.2 It is not an uninteresting fact, that Mr Hume having been introduced by Lord Kames (then Mr Henry Home) to Dr Butler, sent a copy of his Treatise to that philosopher at the moment of his preferment to the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>; and that the perusal of it did not deter the philosophic prelate from "everywhere recommending Mr Hume's Moral and Political Essays,"3 published two years afterwards;—Essays which it would indeed have been unworthy of such a man not to have liberally commended, for they, and those which followed them, whatever may be thought of the contents of some of them, must be ever regarded as the best models in any language, of the short but full, of the clear and agreeable, though deep discussion of difficult questions. Mr Hume considered his Enquiry concerning the Principles of Morals as the best of his writings. It is very creditable to his character, that he should have looked back with most complacency on a Tract the least distinguished by originality, and the least tainted with paradox, among his philosophical works; but deserving of all commendation for the elegant perspicuity of the style, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of illustration and inference with which he unfolded to general readers a doctrine too simple, too certain, and too important, to remain till his time undiscovered among philosophers. His diction has, indeed, neither the grace of Berkeley nor the strength of Hobbes; but it is without the verbosity of the former, or the rugged sternness of the latter. His manner is more lively, more easy, more ingratiating, and, if the word may --- 1 This maxim, which contains a sufficient answer to all universal scepticism, or, in other words, to all scepticism properly so called, is significantly conveyed in the quaint <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of an old and rare book, entitled, Sezis, sive Sceptici et Scepticorum a Jure Dignitatis Exclusio, by Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">White</a>, the metaphysician of the English Catholics in modern times.—"Fortunately," says the illustrious sceptic himself, "since Reason is incapable of dispelling these <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, Nature herself suffices for that purpose, and cures me of this philosophical delirium" (Treatise of Human Nature, I. 467); almost in the sublime and immortal words of Pascal: La Religion confond les Dignitaires, et la Nature les Sceptiques. 2 It would be an act of injustice to those readers who are not acquainted with that valuable volume entitled, Essays on the Formation of Opinions, not to refer them to it as enforcing that neglected part of morality. To it may be added, a masterly article in the Westminster Review, occasioned by the Essays. 3 Woodhouselee's Life of Kames, I. 95, 104. be so applied, more amusing, than that of any other metaphysical writer. He knew himself too well to be, as Dr Johnson asserted, an imitator of Voltaire; who, as it were, embodied in his own person all the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and quickness and versatile ingenuity of a people which surpasses other nations in these brilliant qualities. If he must be supposed to have had an eye on any French writer, it would be a more plausible guess, that he sometimes copied, with a temperate hand, the unexpected thoughts and familiar expressions of Fontenelle. Though he carefully weeded his writings in their successive editions, yet they still contain Scotticisms and Gallicisms enough to employ the successors of such critics as those who exulted over the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PATAVINITY">Patavinity</a> of the Roman Historian. His own great and modest mind would have been satisfied with the praise which cannot be withheld from him, that there is no writer in our language who, through long works, is more agreeable; and it is no derogation from him, that, as a Scotsman, he did not reach those native and secret beauties, characteristic of a language, which are never attained, in elaborate composition, but by a very small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those who familiarly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> in it from infancy. The Enquiry affords perhaps the best specimen of his style. In substance, its chief merit is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, from an abundant enumeration of particulars, that all the qualities and actions of the mind which are generally approved by mankind agree in the circumstance of being useful to society. In the proof, (scarcely necessary) that benevolent affections and actions have that tendency, he asserts the real existence of these affections with unusual warmth; and he well abridges some of the most forcible arguments of Butler, whom it is remarkable that he does not mention. To show the importance of his principle, he very unnecessarily distinguishes the comprehensive duty of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, from other parts of morality, as an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> virtue, for which our respect is solely derived from notions of utility. If all things were in such plenty that there could never be a want, or if men were so benevolent as to provide for the wants of others as much as for their own, there would, says he, in neither <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> be any justice, because there would be no need for it. But it is evident that the same reasoning is applicable to every good affection and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> action. None of them could exist if there were no scope for their exercise. If there were no suffering, there could be no pity and no relief. If there were no offences, there could be no placability. If there were no crimes, there could be no mercy. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERANCE">Temperance</a>, prudence, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, are qualities of which the value depends on the evils by which they are respectively exercised. On purity of manners, it must be owned that Mr Hume, though he controverts no rule, yet treats vice with too much <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. It was his general disposition to distrust virtues which are liable to exaggeration, and may be easily counterfeited. The ascetic pursuit of purity, and hypocritical pretences to patriotism, had too much withdrawn the respect of his equally calm and sincere nature from these excellent virtues; more especially as severity in both these respects was often at apparent variance with affection, which can neither be long assumed, nor ever overvalued. Yet it was singular that he who, in his Essay on Polygamy and Divorce, had so --- 1 These commendations are so far from being at variance with the remarks of the late most ingenious Dr Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>, on Mr Hume's "mode of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>," (Enquiry into the Relation of Cause and Effect, 3d ed. 327) that they may rather be regarded as descriptive of those excellencies of which the excess produced the faults of Mr Hume as a mere searcher and teacher; justly, though perhaps erroneously, controverted by Dr Brown. 2 Enquiry, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. ii. part i., especially the concluding paragraphs; those which precede being more his own. 3 "Si nobis, cum ex hac vita migraverimus, in bellum non insulsa, ut fabulas ferant, immortale secum degere liceret, quid opus esset eloquentia, cum judicia nulla ficerent? aut ipsa etiam virtutibus? Nec enim fortitudine indigemus, nullo proposito aut labore aut periculo; nec justitia, cum eact nihil quod appeteret alieni; nec temperantia, qua respet cas quae nullae essent illibidines; nec prudentia quidem egregia, nullo proposito delectu bonorum et malorum. Una igitur essentiae beati cognitione rerum et scientia." (CICERO. Fragm. ap. AUGUSTIN. de Trinit. iv. 2.) Cicero is more extensive, and therefore more consistent, than Hume; but his enumeration errs both by excess and defect. He supposes knowledge to render beings happy in this imaginary state, without stooping to inquire how. He omits a virtue which might well exist in it, though we cannot conceive its formation in such a state—the delight in each other's wellbeing; and he omits a conceivable though unknown vice, that of unmixed ill-will, which would render such a state a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELL">hell</a> to the wretch who harboured the malevolence. 4 Essays and Treatises, vol I. well shown the connection of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> ties with the outward order of society, should not have perceived their deeper and closer relation to all the social feelings of human nature. It cannot be enough regretted, that, in an Enquiry written with a very moral purpose, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of making truth attractive, by throwing over her the dress of paradox, should have given him for a moment the appearance of weighing the mere amusements of society and conversation against domestic fidelity, which is the preserver of domestic affection, the source of parental fondness and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> regard, and, indirectly, of all the kindness which exists between human beings. That families are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> where the infant heart learns to love, and that pure manners are the cement which alone holds these schools together, are truths so certain, that it is wonderful he should not have betrayed a stronger sense of their importance. No one could so well have proved that all the virtues of that class, in their various orders and degrees, minister to the benevolent affections; and that every act which separates the senses from the affections tends, in some degree, to deprive kindness of its natural auxiliary, and to lessen its prevalence in the world. It did not require his sagacity to discover that the gentlest and tenderest feelings flourish only under the stern guardianship of these severe virtues. Perhaps his philosophy was loosened, though his life was untainted, by that universal and undistinguishing profligacy which prevailed on the Continent, from the regency of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> to the French revolution; the most dissolute period of European history, at least since the Roman emperors. At Rome, indeed, the connection of licentiousness with cruelty, which, though scarcely traceable in individuals, is generally very observable in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses, bore a fearful testimony to the value of austere purity. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> of these remote vices seemed to be broken in the time of Mr Hume. Pleasure, in a more improved state of society, seemed to return to her more natural union with kindness and tenderness, as well as with refinement and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>. Had he lived fourteen years longer, however, he would have seen, that the virtues which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the natural seminaries of the affections are their only true and lasting friends. The demand of all well-informed men for the improvement of civil institutions—the demand of classes of men growing in intelligence, to be delivered from a degrading inferiority, and admitted to a share of political power proportioned to their new importance, being feebly yet violently resisted by those ruling Castes who neither knew how to yield nor how to withstand—being also attended by very erroneous principles of legislation, having suddenly broken down the barriers (imperfect as these were) of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and government, led to popular excesses, desolating wars, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> dictatorship, which for a long time threatened to defeat the reformation, and to disappoint the hopes of mankind. This tremendous convulsion threw a fearful light on the ferocity which lies hid under the arts and pleasures of corrupted nations; as earthquakes and volcanoes disclose the layers which compose the deeper parts of our planet, beneath a fertile and flowery surface. A part of this dreadful result may be ascribed, not improbably, to that relaxation of domestic ties, unhappily natural to the populace of vast capitals, and at that time countenanced and aggravated by the example of their superiors. Another part doubtless arose from the barbarizing power of absolute government, or, in other words, of injustice in high places. A very large portion attests, as strongly as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman history</a>, though in a somewhat different manner, the humanizing efficacy of the family virtues, by the consequences of the want of them in the higher classes, whose profuse and ostentatious sensuality inspired the laborious and suffering portion of mankind with contempt, disgust, envy, and hatred. The Enquiry is disfigured by another speck of more frivolous paradox. It consists in the attempt to give the name of virtue to qualities of the understanding; and it would not have deserved the single remark about to be made on it, had it been the paradox of an inferior man. He has altogether omitted the circumstance on which depends the difference of our sentiments regarding moral and intellectual qualities. We --- 1 See Notes and Illustrations, note R. admire intellectual excellence, but we bestow no moral approbation on it. Such approbation has no tendency directly to increase it, because it is not voluntary. We cultivate our natural disposition to esteem and love benevolence and justice, because these moral sentiments, and the expression of them, directly and materially dispose others, as well as ourselves, to cultivate these two virtues. We cultivate a natural <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> against oppression, which guards ourselves against the practice of that vice, and because the manifestation of it deters others from its exercise. The first rude resentment of a child is against every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of hurt. We confine it to intentional hurt, when we are taught by experience that it prevents only that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of hurt; and at last it is still further limited to wrong done to ourselves or others, and in that case becomes a purely moral sentiment. We morally approve industry, desire of knowledge, love of truth, and all the habits by which the understanding is strengthened and rectified, because their formation is subject to the will. But we do not feel a moral anger against folly or ignorance, because they are involuntary.
